definition: Erudite means having or showing great learning.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word erudite. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know erudite should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The pub quiz banned Mr. Okonjo's table after his erudite streak settled forty questions in a row, from popes to particle physics.
Knowledgeable stops short of erudite: it covers one field handled well — the mechanic who knows engines cold — while erudite ranges across many fields, deep enough to connect what it finds.
Encyclopedic goes further than erudite — the erudite historian has read deeply and can weigh what she read; an encyclopedic memory simply stores it all, weighed or not.

Learned is the plain-English twin of erudite, praising the same deep study in quieter dress: a learned judge, a learned commentary. It fits ordinary speech, while erudite arrives gowned and footnoted, suggesting learning that crosses whole fields and enjoys showing its shelves. The difference is register, not amount.

Bookish means fond of books and the reading life — a bookish teenager haunts the library — but it makes no claim the reading stuck or became learning. Erudite is the proven result: knowledge wide and deep enough to cross fields. A person can stay bookish for decades without turning erudite.

Erudite is the precise word because it means having or showing great learning — learning wide enough to cross fields and deep enough to connect them.
Educated says you finished the courses; erudite says the library moved in.
The word can tip toward showing off, but at its best it names knowledge worn generously.
Erudite praises learning itself — the footnoted, many-fielded kind.
Its unit-mates measure different things: astute reads the moment, acumen judges the deal, nuance is what erudite readers catch in a text.
Learned does the same job in plainer dress; erudite is the word wearing the gown.

Visitors expect the volunteer guide at the tiny maritime museum to know about ships.

But follow his tour for an hour and the ships become doorways: a knot leads him to the mathematics of braids, a ship's biscuit to the chemistry of preservation, a sea shanty to the economics of cotton.
He reads six languages and will cheerfully tell you which dictionary taught him each one.
One reviewer called the tour erudite, and meant it precisely: not a man who knows one subject, but a man whose subjects open onto each other.
The museum's whole collection fits in four rooms.
Nobody has ever seen the same tour twice.
